course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans
lesson.summary: How alliances, trade, and war shaped relations among American Indian nations and French, Dutch, British, and Spanish colonies, including Metacom's War and the Pueblo Revolt.
learningGoals: Explain how European empires and American Indian nations formed alliances and why those alliances produced both cooperation and conflict.
Explain the causes and effects of Metacom's War.
Explain the Pueblo Revolt and how Spain accommodated some aspects of Pueblo culture afterward.
lesson.bigIdea: American Indian nations acted for their own interests, forming alliances and fighting wars with European colonies, and their resistance shaped how colonial societies developed.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how and why interactions between European nations and American Indians changed over time. When you read a source about these events, ask who wrote it, for whom, and why, because each side saw events differently.

sections.title: Alliances and accommodation

blocks.text: Interactions between European rivals and American Indian nations fostered both accommodation and conflict. French, Dutch, British, and Spanish colonies allied with and armed American Indian groups, and Native nations frequently sought alliances with Europeans against other American Indian nations.

The French and their Algonquin and Huron allies fought the Iroquois Confederacy, also called the Haudenosaunee, which traded with the Dutch at Fort Orange and later with the English. In the late 1600s the Iroquois and English colonists joined in a diplomatic alliance known as the Covenant Chain. In Virginia, the Powhatan Confederacy traded with Jamestown's settlers, but conflicts over land and food led to wars, including a Powhatan attack in 1622 that killed hundreds of colonists.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: American Indians were not passive partners. Nations chose alliances to protect their land and trade, and they often bargained with several European powers at once.

sections.takeaway: Europeans and American Indians formed alliances for their own purposes, and those alliances brought both cooperation and conflict.

sections.title: Metacom's War

blocks.text: By the 1670s English settlements in New England had grown, and colonists were pressing onto Native land, extending English law over Native peoples, and pushing Native communities to adopt Christianity. Metacom, a Wampanoag leader whom the English called King Philip, resisted these pressures. In 1675 fighting began after the English executed three Wampanoag men, and it spread across New England as the Wampanoag, Narragansett, Nipmuc, and other nations attacked English towns.

Colonists, aided by Native allies such as the Mohegan, struck back, and the war ended in 1676 when Metacom was killed. Thousands of people died, including a large share of the colonial and Native populations, and English towns were destroyed. British conflicts with American Indians over land, resources, and political boundaries had led to a military confrontation, and its outcome broke the power of Native nations in southern New England, where many captives were enslaved or sold.

sections.takeaway: Conflict over land and authority led to Metacom's War, which devastated both sides and ended Native power in southern New England.

sections.title: The Pueblo Revolt and Spanish accommodation
sections.conceptTitle: The Pueblo Revolt and Spanish accommodation

blocks.text: In New Mexico, Spanish colonists demanded labor and tribute from Pueblo peoples, and Franciscan priests tried to suppress Native religious ceremonies. In 1680, Pueblo communities, led in part by a religious leader named Popé, rose together, killed hundreds of Spanish colonists, including many priests, and drove the Spanish out of New Mexico.

The Spanish returned in 1692 and 1693, but Pueblo resistance changed their approach. Spanish officials reduced forced labor demands and tolerated some Pueblo religious practices alongside Catholicism. American Indian resistance, particularly after the Pueblo Revolt, led to Spanish accommodation of some aspects of American Indian culture in the Southwest.

sections.takeaway: The Pueblo Revolt expelled the Spanish for a time and led Spain to accommodate some Pueblo culture after its return.

connections.title: Forced labor in the British colonies
connections.body: Wars and disease reduced Native populations, and English colonists increasingly relied on enslaved Africans for labor. Topic 2.6 follows how slavery grew and how enslaved people responded.
connections.transferQuestion: How did Native resistance in 1675 and 1680 resemble each other, and how did the results differ?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that both responded to colonial demands for land, labor, or religion, but that Native power ended in southern New England while the Pueblos expelled the Spanish and later gained accommodation.
